title: Progressive JSON checkpoints and deterministic tool callbacks - acceptance criteria and scope
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Purpose: Define clear acceptance criteria and an implementation scope for a progressive JSON checkpointing protocol and deterministic tool-callback semantics when Redwood-hosted models emit structured output and invoke external tools. This ticket captures product requirements, trade-offs, non-goals, and operational considerations so engineering, design, and QA can align on a single implementation plan.

Background: Customers running conversational chains and extraction pipelines have reported two recurring classes of failures: (1) parsers failing due to partial/fragmented JSON emitted over streams and (2) at-least-once tool invocation semantics that lead to duplicate side-effects when model retries occur. The proposed solution introduces a light-weight checkpoint envelope emitted incrementally (checkpoint fragments) and an idempotent deterministic callback contract for tool invocation that is compatible with streaming and non-streaming inference modes.

Scope summary:
- Deliver a protocol for progressive JSON checkpoints (length-prefixed fragments with monotonic fragment_id and finalization marker).
- Define deterministic tool-callback contract (idempotency tokens, logical op IDs, explicit ACK/NACK semantics).
- Add SDK helpers in Node and Python for assembling checkpoints and replaying partial states.
- Add acceptance tests and end-to-end QA runbook that covers network interruptions and consumer reconnection.
- Provide Console-level telemetry (per-request fragment count, retry count, duplicate-callbacks metric) and a short doc for customers.

Out of scope: streaming binary attachments, multimodal media chunking, and protocol-level encryption changes (KMS/HSM remain unchanged).
acceptance_criteria: Checkpoint format: model may emit zero or more checkpoint fragments followed by a final fragment where 'final':true. Each fragment is a top-level JSON object prefixed by a 4-byte length token in bytes. Fragments must include 'fragment_id' (monotonic integer), 'request_id' (UUID), and 'partial_state' (object or null).

Reassembly: SDK must reliably reassemble fragments into a single canonical JSON object when all fragments are present. Reassembly must be deterministic: ordering by fragment_id and field-merging is defined to prefer later fragments for conflicting keys.

Graceful partials: Consumers must be able to accept partial_state snapshots. If the stream is cut before final fragment, the SDK surfaces 'partial=true' and 'final=false' and exposes the highest fragment_id received.

Backpressure and reconnection: If a client reconnects using the same request_id within 30s and provides the last-seen fragment_id, the server must resume sending subsequent fragments or deliver a concise reconciliation payload. This behavior must be documented and tested.

Deterministic callback contract: Tool invocations must include 'op_id' (UUID), 'idempotency_token' (opaque string), and a declared 'side_effects' list. Redwood must guarantee at-most-once observable side-effect execution when a consumer acknowledges success. Retries without ACK may occur but must be marked as 'replay' attempts and not re-apply idempotent side-effects if the tool reports idempotency support.

Explicit ACK/NACK: Tool providers must be able to send structured ACK or NACK messages back to Redwood. ACK must include 'op_id' and 'applied':true. NACK must include 'op_id' and an 'error_code' from a documented set (TRANSIENT, PERMANENT, CONFLICT). Redwood must surface these codes in logs and UI.

Streaming and non-streaming parity: Same logical contract (fragment ids, op ids, idempotency tokens, ACK/NACK) must work for both stream-mode and full-response (non-streamed) inference with equivalent end-state semantics.

SDK helper coverage: Node and Python SDKs include: fragment reassembler, reconnection helper, idempotent callback wrapper, and a simulator test harness that can inject partial fragments and duplicates.

Automated tests: CI includes unit tests for reassembly logic, integration tests for resume/reconnect behavior, and end-to-end tests exercising duplicate tool callback protection. Tests must assert no duplicate side-effect application for a canonical idempotent tool implementation.

Telemetry: Console shows per-request metrics (fragments_sent, fragments_received, reconnections, duplicate_callbacks, percent_finalized). Alerts: duplicate_callbacks > 0.5% triggers P1 investigation runbook.
Docs: Customer-facing guide with examples for Node/Python showing how to consume progressive checkpoints and best practices for tool providers to implement ACK/NACK and idempotency.
Security review: Because the protocol surfaces op ids and fragments across network reconnections, a security review note must be captured and security_review_required set to true for final sign-off.
non_goals: Change persistent storage formats for existing audit logs (we will adapt exporters instead).
Implement cross-region multi-master fragment replication (out of scope for initial launch).
Support arbitrary binary payload streaming (only structured JSON checkpointing is supported).
implementation_notes: Protocol design: use a text-based JSON fragment wrapped with a 4-byte BE length prefix to ensure stream boundaries are unambiguous over HTTP/2 and websockets.
Fragments schema: { request_id, fragment_id, partial_state, final:boolean, checkpoint_ts_iso }

Tool callback flow: model emits structured call -> Redwood routes to tool gateway with op_id and idempotency_token -> tool responds with ACK/NACK -> Redwood surfaces result and reconciles state with fragment emissions.
Retries: default retry window 30s for reconnection-based resume. Retries outside window should trigger a reconciliation payload (complete state snapshot).

SDK behavior: reassembly must tolerate duplicate fragments and drop duplicates by fragment_id. Later fragments overwrite conflicting keys. Consumers can subscribe to 'checkpoint' events for optimistic UI updates.

success_metrics: <1% parser failures for customers using checkpoints after 30 days
>= 90% of resumed connections successfully reconcile state within 5s
risks: Runtime performance: length-prefix parsing adds negligible overhead but must be validated at high QPS.
Tool provider adoption: providers must implement ACK/NACK and idempotency which may slow partner integrations.
SDK complexity: reassembly and conflict resolution edge cases could lead to subtle bugs if not exhaustively tested.
